title: Multiscale Mechanisms Governing the Performance Evolution of MgO-GGBS-Stone Powder Lightweight Foamed Soil Under CO 2  Curing
abstract: Abstract To facilitate low-carbon construction technologies in subgrade engineering, this study proposes a carbon-sequestering lightweight foamed soil (C-LFS) using an all-solid-waste binder system in which reactive magnesium oxide (MgO), ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS), and stone powder (SP) fully replace Portland cement. Specimens with target wet densities of 600–800 kg/m 3  were prepared, and macroscopic tests on workability and early setting, dry density, and unconfined compressive strength (UCS) were conducted. SEM and XRD characterization were further performed to reveal carbonation-driven product evolution and microstructural changes. The results show that increasing MgO dosage decreases slurry flowability and shortens setting time. The 28-day UCS exhibits a rise-then-fall trend with both MgO dosage and water-to-binder ratio. At a wet density of 700 kg/m 3 , the optimum MgO dosage and water-to-binder ratio are 35% and 0.65, respectively, yielding a maximum 28-day UCS of 1.132 MPa. Carbonation curing markedly enhances CO 2  uptake and carbonate formation, demonstrating promising CO 2  mineralization potential, with a CO 2  uptake of approximately 67.3 kg CO 2 /t after 5 days of carbonation. However, with prolonged carbonation, the pore-solution pH drops rapidly, suppressing sustained GGBS activation and late-stage MgO hydration; this in turn induces gel-framework weakening (decalcification of C-(A)-S-H), pore-structure coarsening, and microcrack development, causing UCS to decrease continuously with carbonation age, with more pronounced degradation under the combined condition of high MgO dosage and extended carbonation. Despite strength degradation, the 28-day UCS can still be maintained at 0.752 MPa, meeting the strength requirements for subgrade filling. Overall, this study elucidates the trade-off mechanism between CO 2  mineralization and mechanical performance of C-LFS from coupled macro-meso-micro perspectives, providing guidance for the design and application of low-carbon lightweight foamed soil in subgrade backfill and a basis for optimizing the carbonation-curing regime of this material.
journal: International Journal of Concrete Structures and Materials

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Foamed lightweight soil (FLS) has been widely used in subgrade engineering because of its low density, good flowability, and ease of placement. In practical applications such as subgrade backfilling, embankment widening, backfilling behind structures, and soft-ground treatment, FLS can effectively reduce self-weight-induced additional stress and differential settlement while maintaining construction efficiency and adaptability (Amran et al.,  1 ; Chen et al.,  7 ; Kim et al.,  20 ; Ni et al.,  27 ; Shi et al.,  32 ; Yuan et al.,  37 ). These characteristics make FLS an attractive candidate for transportation infrastructure where lightweight filling and construction convenience are simultaneously required. However, conventional FLS still relies primarily on ordinary Portland cement (OPC) as the main binder, and its large-scale use is therefore associated with considerable clinker consumption and embodied CO 2  emissions. Meanwhile, large quantities of fine solid wastes, especially stone powder generated during manufactured-sand production and rock processing, remain underutilized in high-value geotechnical materials. Developing a low-clinker or cement-free FLS system that can simultaneously reduce binder-related carbon emissions and valorize such fine solid wastes is thus of clear practical significance for sustainable subgrade construction (Lei et al.,  21 ; Orsini & Marrone,  28 ; Zhang et al.,  38 ).

Reactive MgO is a promising component for such systems. Compared with OPC clinker, reactive MgO can be produced at relatively low calcination temperatures and exhibits inherent carbonation reactivity, offering additional CO2 mineralization potential during curing (Cai et al.,  6 ; Guan et al.,  12 ; Li & Yi,  23 ; Shen et al.,  31 ; Yi et al.,  36 ). MgO-based carbonation routes have been successfully applied in soil improvement, contaminated-soil stabilization, and carbonation-based ground treatment, although the treatment effect is highly sensitive to MgO reactivity or dosage, water condition, and carbonation duration (Cai et al.,  6 ; Guan et al.,  12 ; Li & Yi,  23 ; Shen et al.,  31 ; Yi et al.,  36 ). Nevertheless, most existing studies have focused on relatively dense soil matrices, whereas the reaction evolution and performance response in highly porous foamed materials remain insufficiently understood.

Against this background, a cement-free binder system based on reactive MgO, ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS), and stone powder (SP) provides a promising route for the development of low-carbon lightweight foamed soil. In such a system, SP mainly acts as a filler and particle-grading regulator (Bagheri & Samea,  4 ; Zhang et al.,  39 ), whereas GGBS should be regarded as a latent hydraulic precursor that requires activation under an alkaline environment (Jin et al.,  17 ; Park et al.,  29 ). MgO is particularly important because it can not only provide the alkalinity required for slag activation through hydration, but can also participate in carbonation mineralization (Mo & Panesar,  24 ). Therefore, CO 2  curing is introduced in this study not as a simple strength-enhancing curing method, but as a controllable early-age mineralization strategy for a cement-free foamed system. On the one hand, carbonation of Mg-bearing and Ca-bearing phases may improve the CO 2  sequestration capacity of the material. On the other hand, CO 2  ingress may reduce pore-solution alkalinity, suppress sustained slag activation and later-age reaction development, and destabilize the gel-based load-bearing skeleton (Azar et al.,  2 ; Li et al.,  22 ). Accordingly, for such a highly porous foamed material, the relationship between CO 2  mineralization and mechanical performance is expected to be governed by a trade-off rather than a simple synergy.

To address, this issue, this study develops a carbon-sequestering lightweight foamed soil (C-LFS) using MgO, GGBS, and SP to fully replace Portland cement in the binder system for lightweight subgrade backfill. Laboratory tests were conducted to investigate the effects of MgO dosage, GGBS content, water-to-binder ratio, target wet density, and carbonation duration on the workability, dry density, unconfined compressive strength, pore-structure evolution, reaction–product transformation, and CO 2  uptake of the material. Particular emphasis is placed on clarifying the multiscale mechanism behind the seemingly contradictory phenomenon that carbonation enhances CO 2  mineralization but continuously reduces strength. The results are expected to provide a theoretical basis for mix design and for the selection of appropriate carbonation-curing boundaries for low-carbon lightweight foamed geomaterials in subgrade engineering (Fig.  1 ). sections.heading: Mix Design
paragraphs:
Reactive MgO used in this study was supplied by Chengdu Construction Engineering Group (Chengdu, China), with a specific surface area of 22 m 2 /g and a density of 3.65 g/cm 3 . Ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) was obtained from Chengdu Construction Engineering Group, with a grade of S95. Stone powder (SP), collected from limestone parent rock, was used as the filler component. The foaming agent was obtained from Guangdong Chengxin Co., Ltd., and deionized water was used for specimen preparation. The chemical compositions of MgO, GGBS, and SP were determined by XRF, and their main physical properties are summarized in Table  1 . The particle-size distribution, mineral composition, and microstructural features of the raw materials are shown in Fig.  2 .
 Table 1 Main chemical compositions of raw materials (%) Material CaO SiO 2 Al 2 O 3 MgO Fe 2 O 3 SO 3 Others GGBS 39.8 34.6 12.5 7.8 0.7 0.2 3.4 MgO 1.5 0.8 0.3 94.2 0.2 0.1 2.9 SP 54.2 35.7 3.6 1.2 0.8 0.3 4.2 Fig. 2 The particle size, mineral composition, and microstructure of the various materials

With reference to the typical wet-density range used for foamed lightweight soil in railway and highway engineering (approximately 500–800 kg/m 3  (China Ministry of Railways of the People's Republic of China, Q/CR 758–2020,  9 ; China Ministry of Railways of the People's Republic of China, T/CHCA 001–2021,  10 ) three representative target wet densities, namely 600, 700, and 800 kg/m 3 , were selected in this study. These three levels correspond to relatively low, medium, and relatively high lightweight grades within the practical engineering window for subgrade backfill. The lower bound was set at 600 kg/m 3  because a further reduction in wet density would require a higher foam volume, which tends to produce thinner pore walls and a less stable load-bearing skeleton in this cement-free MgO-GGBS-SP system. The upper bound was set at 800 kg/m 3  to retain the lightweight advantage of the material for subgrade applications. Therefore, the selected range was intended to balance engineering representativeness, lightweight effect, and mechanical comparability. Based on previous findings on the influence of MgO content on carbonation performance (Iqra et al.,  16 ; Mo & Panesar,  24 ; Zhang et al.,  40 ), an MgO content range of 25–45% was adopted, with an increment of 5%. To maximize the resource utilization of manufactured sand stone powder, a series of preliminary tests were carried out, which revealed pronounced surface scaling when the stone powder content exceeded 30%; therefore, the content of manufactured sand stone powder was set in the range of 10–30%. In the present study, the binder composition was constrained by MgO + GGBS + SP = 100%. Therefore, the experimental program was not a full orthogonal design with mutually independent binder fractions, but a grouped parametric study under a constant-binder-sum constraint. In the MgO series, MgO was varied while GGBS was fixed and SP was adjusted correspondingly. In the GGBS series, GGBS was varied, while MgO was fixed and SP was adjusted correspondingly. The detailed design matrix is summarized in Table  2 .

sections.heading: Specimen Preparation and Maintenance
paragraphs: The raw materials are weighed and mixed according to the designed proportions, and the resulting mixture is then poured into cubic molds (100 × 100 × 100 mm) and cylindrical molds (50 mm in diameter and 100 mm in height). All specimens were tested at a fixed total curing age of 28 days. For the carbonation groups, the specimens were subjected to CO 2  curing for 0, 1, 3, or 5 days during the curing period, and were then transferred to standard curing conditions until the total curing age reached 28 days before strength testing. The 0-day group was kept under standard curing conditions throughout the entire 28-day period. The standard curing conditions were a constant temperature of 22 ± 2 °C and a relative humidity of 95%, while the CO 2  curing conditions were a CO 2  concentration of 20 ± 2%, a temperature of 22 ± 2 °C, and a relative humidity of 90 ± 2%. The specimen preparation and curing process is shown in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 Specimen preparation and maintenance

sections.heading: Flow Value
paragraphs: The test was carried out with reference to the Technical Specification for Cast-in-Place Lightweight foamed soil (CECS 249:2008). A steel cylinder with an inner diameter of 8 cm, an effective height of 8 cm, and a wall thickness of 0.2 cm, together with a square plastic plate with a side length of 30 cm and a thickness of 1 cm, was used. The cylinder was placed vertically on the plastic plate, and the prepared C-LFS slurry was poured into the cylinder until it slightly exceeded the top edge. A scraper was then used to level the slurry flush with the rim of the cylinder. The cylinder was lifted vertically so that all the slurry in the cylinder flowed out onto the plate to form a circular pat, and a stopwatch was started simultaneously. After 1 min, the diameter of the circular pat on the plate was measured with a Vernier caliper, and this value was taken as the flow value of the C-LFS.

sections.heading: Setting Time
paragraphs: The initial and final setting times of C-LFS were measured using a Vicat apparatus. Slurry adjusted to the target wet density was used for the tests, and the arithmetic mean of three measurements was taken as the setting time of the lightweight foamed soil. The initial and final setting times were measured using a Vicat apparatus in accordance with the Technical Specification for Cast-in-Place Lightweight foamed soil (CECS 249:2008).

sections.heading: Unconfined Compressive Strength Test
paragraphs: Unconfined compressive strength tests were conducted on cubic specimens with a side length of 100 mm, in accordance with GB/T 11969-2008 (China Ministry of Railways of the People's Republic of China, GB/T 11969-2008,  8 ). A universal testing machine was used to apply a load at a rate of (10 ± 1) mm/min (China Ministry of Railways of the People's Republic of China, GB/T 11969-2008,  8 ) until the specimen failed. The failure load  P  was recorded, and the maximum compressive stress was calculated. The compressive strength of C-LFS was determined as the average strength of three cubic specimens with the same mix ratio. The unconfined compressive strength test was carried out using a WAW-2000E universal testing machine (Wenteng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., China).

sections.heading: TG-DSC
SEM
paragraphs: The pore structure and microstructural components of the C-LFS were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). For pore-structure analysis, a magnification of 30 × was adopted. After 28 days of curing, the specimens were cut into small rectangular blocks with dimensions of 10 mm in thickness, 10 mm in width, and 20 mm in length using a handheld concrete cutter. Prior to SEM testing, the fragments were dried and sputter-coated with gold. Several images at different magnifications were taken for each specimen. For the images captured at 30 × magnification, ImageJ was used to process the images and calculate the geometrical parameters of the pore structure, including pore size, area, and circularity. For the low-magnification SEM images, the reported porosity was calculated as the sectional pore-area fraction obtained by image segmentation in ImageJ. In addition, magnifications of 6000 and 12,000 were used to observe the microstructural components of the C-LFS. SEM observations were conducted using a Hitachi Regulus8100 scanning electron microscope (Shanghai Huiyan Technology Co., Ltd., China).

sections.heading: FTIR
paragraphs: FTIR was used to track carbonation products and gel evolution in C-LFS. As the carbonation age increased, the carbonate-related absorption bands intensified, indicating continuous carbonate formation, whereas the relative Si-O-T band associated with the gel framework weakened. To semi-quantitatively compare these two competing trends, the FTIR proxy ratio  R FTIR  was defined according to Eq. ( 4 ), using the baseline-corrected integrated area of the carbonate-related band and that of the gel-related Si-O-T band. The same baseline-correction procedure and integration windows were used for all spectra to ensure comparability. FTIR spectra were recorded using a Nicolet iS 10 spectrometer (Scientific Compass, China).

sections.heading: XRD
paragraphs: XRD was conducted to determine the crystalline phase assemblage of the lightweight foamed soil after 28-day curing, distinguishing hydration products from unreacted precursors and qualitatively tracking reaction progress. Particular attention was paid to CaCO 3  polymorphs, Mg-bearing phases. XRD patterns were collected using an X'Pert PRO MPD diffractometer (Scientific Compass, China) with Cu Kα radiation. For semi-quantitative tracking of the amorphous gel contribution, the broad hump in the 20–40° 2θ range was fitted in Origin using a single Gaussian function after linear baseline subtraction. The fitting range was fixed at 20–40° for all specimens to ensure comparability. The hump area and peak intensity were extracted from the fitted curve and then normalized to the 0-day specimen. The goodness-of-fit was evaluated using the coefficient of determination. This fitting was intended to track the overall evolution of the amorphous gel-related contribution rather than to resolve individual overlapping crystalline peaks. For semi-quantitative tracking of the amorphous gel contribution, the broad hump in the 20–40° 2θ range was fitted in Origin using a single Gaussian function after linear baseline subtraction. The fitting range was fixed at 20–40° for all specimens to ensure comparability. The fitted hump area and peak intensity were extracted from the fitted curve and normalized to the 0-day specimen. The XRD hump index H XRD  was defined according to Eq. ( 5 ) using the normalized hump area, while the normalized hump peak intensity was reported as a supplementary descriptor.

sections.heading: Isothermal Calorimetry
paragraphs: For different carbonation ages, the calorimetry tests were conducted on fresh pastes mixed with extracted pore solutions obtained from specimens carbonated for 0, 1, 3, and 5 days, so as to reproduce the corresponding alkalinity environments and quantify their effects on reaction kinetics. Isothermal calorimetry was conducted using an I-Cal 8000 calorimeter (Shanghai, China).

sections.heading: Definition of Derived Indices
paragraphs: To quantitatively describe the effects of carbonation on reaction persistence, alkalinity-collapse kinetics, phase evolution, and gel-framework degradation, four derived indices were defined in this study.

sections.heading: Flow Value and Setting Time
paragraphs: Fig.  4  shows the variations of flow value and setting time under different MgO contents, target wet densities, water-to-binder ratios, and GGBS contents. As seen in Fig.  4 a, the flow value decreases slowly with increasing MgO content, while both initial and final setting times shorten significantly. This is mainly related to the larger specific surface area and stronger water absorption capacity of MgO particles. A higher MgO content greatly increases the water demand of the system. It reduces the amount of effective free water in the mixture and thus lowers the macroscopic flowability of the slurry. At the same time, increasing MgO enhances the alkalinity of the pore solution. This provides more favorable conditions for activating GGBS. GGBS is more effectively activated and participates in latent hydraulic and pozzolanic-type reactions under the alkaline environment provided by MgO, forming a large amount of C-(A)-S-H and other gel products. These gels build bridge-like structures between particles and accelerate the transition from a “flowing slurry” to a “continuous skeleton.” As a result, both the initial and final setting times are significantly reduced. This interpretation is consistent with previous studies showing that increasing reactive MgO generally reduces the workability of slag-rich systems because of its higher water demand, while also accelerating early hydration, shortening setting time, and promoting the formation of C-(A)-S-H- and hydrotalcite-related binding phases under alkaline conditions (He et al.,  13 ; Huang et al.,  14 ; Hwang et al.,  15 ). Fig. 4 MgO relationships of MgO content, target wet density, water-to-binder ratio, and GGBS content with flow value and setting time:  a  Relationship between MgO content and flow value and setting time,  b  relationship between target wet density and flow value and setting time,  c  relationship between water-to-binder ratio and flow value and setting time,  d  relationship between GGBS content and flow value and setting time

As shown in Fig.  4 b and c, when the target wet density increases, the flow value increases slightly, while the setting time decreases overall. This behavior is closely related to the foam content. At a lower target wet density, more foam must be introduced to achieve the required dry density. This means a large amount of gaseous voids is added to the system. These voids weaken the integrity of the continuous paste skeleton and reduce the self-weight flow capacity of the slurry. As a result, the spread diameter in the flow test is limited, and the macroscopic flow value is relatively low. With increasing target wet density, the foam content decreases accordingly. The proportion of the continuous liquid–solid skeleton increases, and the self-weight effect of the slurry is enhanced. The slurry can spread more easily on the flow table, so the flow value increases slightly. On the other hand, when the water-to-binder ratio is kept essentially constant, increasing the target wet density in essence increases the absolute amount of binders (MgO, GGBS) and the number of reaction sites per unit volume. This raises the concentration and supersaturation of Ca 2+ , Mg 2+  and Si, Al species in the pore solution. C-(A)-S-H gel, Mg(OH) 2 , and carbonate phases can therefore nucleate and grow more rapidly and form bridging structures between particles. This accelerates the transition from a “flowing slurry” to a “load-bearing skeleton,” so both the initial and final setting times tend to decrease. When the water-to-binder ratio increases, the flow value rises markedly, while the setting time is significantly prolonged. This reflects the typical rule of “more water, higher flowability but slower setting.” A higher water-to-binder ratio provides more free water to lubricate particle surfaces and reduce plastic viscosity, which greatly improves the flowability of the slurry. However, the excess water dilutes the concentrations of OH⁻, Ca 2+ , Mg 2+ , and other ions in the system. This weakens the driving force for hydration. It also increases the average interparticle distance and reduces the effective contact frequency between particles. The formation of the structural skeleton is therefore delayed, leading to longer initial and final setting times. The observed influence of foam content and water-to-binder ratio on flowability and setting is also generally consistent with the reported behavior of foamed concrete and slag-based alkali-activated systems, in which foam dosage affects the stability and mobility of the fresh cellular matrix, whereas increasing the liquid/binder ratio tends to reduce viscosity and modify setting and structural build-up kinetics (Dai et al.,  11 ; Yao et al.,  35 ; Zhang et al.,  41 ).

As shown in Fig.  4 d unlike MgO, increasing the GGBS content causes little change in the flow value, while both the initial and final setting times show a decreasing trend. This indicates that, within the dosage range used in this study, GGBS has a relatively mild influence on the workability of the mixture. On the one hand, most GGBS particles are in a glassy state and have relatively smooth surfaces. Their fineness is close to that of the base cementitious materials. Thus, the water demand does not increase significantly, and the flow value remains almost unchanged. On the other hand, under the high-pH environment and Ca 2+  supply provided by MgO, the latent hydraulic reactivity of GGBS is more effectively activated. C-(A)-S-H gel forms more rapidly, which shortens the setting time. These observations are consistent with previous studies reporting that slag under strong alkali activation helps accelerate early structural formation.

Overall, by reasonably adjusting the MgO and GGBS contents, as well as the water-to-binder ratio and target wet density, the C-LFS slurry can achieve adequate flowability. At the same time, the setting time can be controlled within a suitable construction window. This provides favorable conditions for subsequent molding and carbonation curing.

sections.heading: Dry Density
paragraphs: Fig.  5  shows the variation of dry density of C-LFS at 7, 14, and 28 days under different MgO contents, target wet densities, water-to-binder ratios, and carbonation durations. It can be seen that, with increasing curing age, the dry density of all mixes gradually decreases. The values at 7 days are the highest, followed by 14 days, and those at 28 days are the lowest. This indicates that during natural curing and carbonation, continuous water loss and volumetric deformation occur inside the specimens. The combined effect of mass loss and pore coarsening is greater than the densification caused by skeleton shrinkage, so the macroscopic dry density shows a slight decrease. Fig. 5 Relationship of MgO content, target wet density, water-to-binder ratio, and carbonation duration with dry density:  a  Relationship between MgO content and dry density,  b  relationship between target wet density and dry density,  c  relationship between water-to-binder ratio and dry density,  d  relationship between carbonation duration and dry density

From Fig.  5 a it can be observed that, at the same age, increasing the MgO content leads to a slight increase in dry density. This suggests that an appropriate amount of MgO helps form a relatively denser skeleton. However, its influence is clearly weaker than that of target wet density and water-to-binder ratio. Fig.  5 b shows that the dry density increases almost linearly with increasing target wet density. This again confirms that the target wet density is the dominant factor controlling the bulk density of C-LFS. Fig.  5 c indicates that the dry density decreases significantly as the water-to-binder ratio increases. This is consistent with the mechanism whereby a higher water-to-binder ratio leads to higher porosity and a lower solid volume fraction. In Fig.  5 d, at the same curing age, the dry density decreases gradually as the carbonation time increases from 0 to 5 days. This suggests that carbonation in this system does not make the structure denser. On the contrary, the reduction in pH may suppress the later reactions of GGBS and MgO. It may also induce microcracking and the formation of larger pores, which weaken the effective load-bearing skeleton.

Overall, the dry density of C-LFS is mainly controlled by the target wet density and the water-to-binder ratio. MgO content and carbonation duration influence dry density and mechanical properties in a secondary but non-negligible way, by modifying the evolution of the microstructure.

sections.heading: Unconfined Compressive Strength
paragraphs: The variation in unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of the C-LFS blocks is shown in Fig.  6 . In Fig.  6 a when the MgO dosage is taken as the variable, the bar charts for different carbonation ages are approximately parallel. For a given MgO dosage, the UCS is highest at 0-day carbonation, followed by 1 day and 3 days, and reaches the lowest value at 5 days. In addition, as the MgO content increases from 25 to 35%, the 28-day UCS first increases; when the MgO content is further increased, the strength slightly decreases. This indicates that an appropriate MgO dosage helps enhance the stiffness of the load-bearing skeleton, whereas an excessive dosage leads to strength reduction under prolonged carbonation. Fig. 6 Effects of carbonation age, MgO content, and GGBS content on 28-day unconfined compressive strength and pore solution pH of C-LFS:  a  UCS at different MgO contents,  b  UCS at different GGBS contents,  c  UCS at different W/B,  d  UCS at different wet density,  e  radar chart of 28-day UCS, 24-h pH, and 7-day pH at different carbonation ages

Fig.  6 b shows a similar trend for different GGBS dosages. The non-carbonated specimens exhibit significantly higher UCS than those carbonated for 1 day, 3 days, and 5 days, and the strength loss becomes more pronounced with increasing carbonation duration. With increasing GGBS content, the UCS of the 0-day group increases overall, suggesting that the latent hydraulic reactivity of slag is effectively activated under a highly alkaline environment. However, under long-term carbonation, mixtures with higher GGBS contents also show more evident strength loss.

Fig.  6 c further compares UCS at different water-to-binder ratios. In general, at the same carbonation age, increasing the water-to-binder ratio reduces the 28-day UCS. At a fixed water-to-binder ratio, carbonation for 1–5 days causes varying degrees of strength reduction, and the reduction becomes greater as carbonation time increases. This implies that although a higher water-to-binder ratio is beneficial for mixing and foam stability, it increases porosity and pore connectivity, facilitating CO 2  diffusion into pore walls and gel interfaces. As a result, carbonation reactions and chemical alteration of gel phases are accelerated, amplifying the strength-loss effect.

Fig.  6 d presents the UCS variation under different designed wet densities. For the non-carbonated specimens, a higher wet density leads to a higher 28-day UCS, indicating that thicker pore walls and a higher solid volume fraction can significantly improve the load-bearing capacity of the skeleton. Under carbonation curing, however, all density groups exhibit strength decreases, with a more pronounced reduction for the low-density specimens. This is because low-density C-LFS has thinner pore walls and a higher proportion of open pores. Although carbonation precipitation may locally provide a “filling effect,” it cannot offset the adverse effects of gel-skeleton weakening and microcrack development, resulting in a greater overall strength reduction. Overall, Fig.  6 a–d that carbonation curing reduces the UCS of C-LFS regardless of changes in MgO dosage, GGBS dosage, water-to-binder ratio, or wet density. Moreover, the UCS continuously decreases with increasing carbonation time, indicating that strength loss is a general phenomenon primarily driven by carbonation reactions. This behavior differs from that reported for relatively dense Portland-cement-based materials subjected to short-duration early-age carbonation, where carbonate precipitation may densify the matrix and improve early mechanical performance. By contrast, in slag-rich or alkali-activated slag systems, more extensive carbonation is commonly associated with decalcification of the C-(A)-S-H/C-S-H-type gel framework and the accompanying loss of mechanical performance (Bernal et al.,  5 ; Junior et al.,  18 ; Shi et al.,  33 ).

The radar chart in Fig.  6 e compares the 28-day unconfined compressive strength of C-LFS, the pH measured 24 h after mixing, and the pH at 7 days for different carbonation ages. The results indicate that carbonation gradually shifts the pore-solution pH from strongly alkaline toward near-neutral conditions, weakening the sustained activation of MgO and GGBS. Consequently, later-stage hydration is markedly suppressed and the formation of new gel products becomes limited, which significantly slows the strength development of carbonated C-LFS and, for some mix designs, even leads to a certain degree of strength reduction. This pH evolution is consistent with previous studies on slag-based and alkali-activated slag binders, in which carbonation altered pore-solution chemistry, destabilized Ca-rich binding gels, and shortened the effective alkaline window for continued reaction. Similar alkalinity loss and porosity increase under carbonation have also been reported in sodium carbonate-activated slag systems (Azar et al.,  3 ; Nedeljković et al.,  25 ; Nguyen et al.,  26 ).

sections.heading: Carbonation Depth
paragraphs: The C-FLS blocks were sprayed with phenolphthalein solution for color indication, and the appearance of specimens under different carbonation durations is shown in Fig.  7 a. Compared with the non-carbonated specimens, the red-colored area on the surface of the carbonated blocks gradually shrinks, forming a distinct carbonation zone. As the carbonation time increases from 1 to 3 days and 5 days, the carbonated region progressively extends from the surface toward the interior, and its area increases markedly. This indicates that CO 2  has gradually penetrated into the core region. Fig. 7 Surface appearance and carbonation depth of C-LFS specimens under different carbonation durations:  a  Surface appearance,  b  carbonation depth

Fig.  7 b shows that, with increasing MgO dosage, the carbonation depth first decreases and then increases. At relatively low MgO contents, MgO hydrates to form Mg(OH) 2 , which reacts with the infiltrating CO₂ during carbonation to produce hydromagnesite and magnesium carbonate. These products tend to densify the internal structure and hinder further CO 2  diffusion. When the MgO dosage exceeds a certain threshold, however, the carbonation depth increases again. Based on the present data, this behavior is more conservatively attributed to the higher water demand of MgO, reduced foam stability, and the resulting coarser and more connected pore structure, which together facilitate CO 2  ingress. Although local expansive stress related to MgO hydration may also be involved, this possibility was not directly verified in the present study and therefore should be regarded as a hypothesis requiring further validation. This trend is consistent with the earlier observation that the compressive strength first increases and then decreases with increasing MgO content. These results suggest that, as carbonation proceeds, prolonged carbonation leads to greater CO 2  uptake, which in turn contributes to the deterioration of mechanical performance.

sections.heading: Porosity
paragraphs: Fig.  8  shows the evolution of the 28-day porosity of C-LFS blocks with carbonation age. Fig.  8 a indicates that, within the MgO range of 25–45%, the porosity increases slightly with increasing MgO. For a given MgO dosage, the porosity also rises gradually as the carbonation age extends from 0 to 1 day, 3 days, and 5 days. This suggests that higher MgO contents and longer carbonation promote a higher pore volume and a greater proportion of connected pores. This trend may be attributed to the increased water demand and reduced foam stability at high MgO dosages, together with carbonation shrinkage-induced microcrack development, which collectively increase the overall porosity. Fig.  8 b shows that, within the GGBS range of 35–55%, the porosity at 0 day generally decreases with increasing GGBS. A similar decreasing trend is observed at 1 day and 3 days, although the reduction at 3 days becomes less pronounced. By 5 days, the differences among mixes become smaller, and some mixes even show a slight rebound. These results indicate that a moderate increase in GGBS helps refine the pore structure and reduce porosity at early ages, but this refinement effect is partially offset under prolonged carbonation. Fig.  8 c illustrates the influence of the water-to-binder ratio. Increasing w/b raises the porosity at 0 day. At a given w/b, extending the carbonation duration generally increases porosity, implying that a higher w/b produces a looser pore structure and facilitates CO 2  mass transfer, thereby aggravating carbonation-induced pore coarsening and microcrack development. Fig.  8 d shows that, for different designed wet densities, the porosity at 0 day decreases as the wet density increases. After carbonation, porosity increases for all density groups, with a more pronounced increase for low-density specimens. This is mainly because low-density C-LFS has thinner pore walls and more open pores, which provide easier pathways for CO 2  ingress. The present pore response is therefore different from that of some relatively dense cement pastes, in which carbonation may reduce pore volume through CaCO 3  precipitation and partial filling of capillary pores. However, previous studies also indicate that once gel decalcification and pore coarsening become dominant, the net pore response can shift away from densification. In the present highly porous foamed system, skeleton degradation evidently dominates over local filling, resulting in a net increase in porosity with carbonation age (Kim et al.,  19 ; Shah et al.,  30 ; Xian & Shao,  34 ). Fig. 8 Porosity of C-LFS blocks at 28 days as a function of MgO and GGBS contents:  a  Porosity versus MgO content (%),  b  porosity versus GGBS content (%),  c  porosity versus W/B,  d  porosity versus wet density

Overall, although carbonation precipitation may locally fill pores, under the present experimental conditions, the net effect is still pore-structure coarsening and increased microcracking, leading to a gradual increase in porosity with increasing carbonation age. It should be noted that the increase in image-based porosity does not necessarily contradict the local solid-volume expansion associated with carbonate precipitation. In the present highly porous foamed system, carbonate formation may locally provide surface deposition and limited pore filling, whereas the net sectional porosity is governed by the competition between local filling and skeleton degradation, including gel weakening, pore-wall thinning, crack opening, and pore coalescence. Under the present experimental conditions, the latter dominates, leading to an increase in porosity with increasing carbonation age.

sections.heading: Pore Size Distribution
paragraphs: Different MgO contents

Fig.  9  presents the pore size distribution characteristics of C-LFS with different MgO contents and the corresponding statistical results. The micro-morphology images at the top show that all specimens exhibit a typical hierarchical cellular structure dominated by nearly spherical pores. However, the integrity of pore walls and the number of open pores vary with MgO content. The pore-size histograms and fitted curves in the middle indicate that the pore-size distributions of all groups are approximately normal and mainly concentrated in the range of 100–200 μm. The dashed lines marking the mean and median shift with MgO content, reflecting changes in the characteristic pore size. Further, the scatter plots and box plots at the bottom reveal distinct differences in pore-size dispersion among different MgO contents. The 25% MgO group shows a more concentrated distribution with a higher proportion of small pores. When the MgO content increases to 35%, the pore-size distribution becomes the most stable with relatively low dispersion, suggesting a better coordination between pore formation and the supporting pore-wall skeleton at this dosage. When the MgO content is further increased to 45%, the distribution shifts to the right and becomes more dispersed, with more extremely large pores and open pores. This implies that, under high MgO conditions, the increased water demand and reduced foam stability, together with potentially stronger shrinkage mismatch and microcrack development, lead to pore coarsening and enhanced connectivity. Overall, varying MgO content does not change the basic distribution pattern of C-LFS, with pore sizes predominantly in the 100–200 μm range, but it significantly affects the degree of uniformity and the tendency toward pore coarsening. A moderate MgO content (e.g., 35%) helps form a more uniform and stable pore structure, whereas excessive MgO more readily induces pore coalescence and pore-wall defects. These changes provide pathways for CO 2  mass transfer and reactions during subsequent carbonation, thereby amplifying pore-structure reconstruction and strength-loss effects. Different carbonation ages Fig. 9 Pore size distribution of C-LFS with different MgO contents

Fig.  10  shows the pore size distribution characteristics and statistical results of C-LFS at different carbonation ages (0, 1, 3, and 5 days) under the following conditions: MgO content of 35%, GGBS content of 45%, water-to-binder ratio of 0.65, and designed wet density of 700 kg/m 3 . The micro-morphology images at the top indicate that all groups exhibit a typical foamed pore structure dominated by nearly spherical pores. As the carbonation time increases, however, localized roughening of pore walls and an increase in pore-wall defects can be observed. The histograms and fitted curves in the middle show that the pore-size distributions at all ages remain mainly concentrated in the 100–200 μm range and are approximately normal. The dashed lines marking the mean and median shift slightly with carbonation age, reflecting the evolution of the characteristic pore size. The scatter plots and box plots at the bottom further reveal that the 0-day group has a more concentrated distribution with lower dispersion. After 1 day of carbonation, the overall distribution changes only slightly, but the dispersion increases marginally. When carbonation is extended to 3 days and 5 days, the distribution becomes more dispersed, with more extremely large pores and outliers, suggesting enhanced pore coalescence and the development of pore-wall microcracks. Overall, for this representative mix design, short-term carbonation (0 day and 1 day) has a limited influence on the dominant pore-size range, whereas mid–to–late carbonation (3 days, 4 days, and 5 days) more readily induces pore coarsening and increased pore connectivity. This indicates that, although carbonation may cause local carbonate precipitation, the chemical alteration of gel phases and shrinkage incompatibility induced by carbonation are more likely to dominate pore-wall defect propagation, thereby driving pore-structure reconstruction and providing a structural explanation for strength loss. Different water-to-binder ratios Fig. 10 Pore size distribution of C-LFS at different carbonation ages

Fig.  11  shows the pore size distribution characteristics and statistical results of C-LFS with different water-to-binder ratios (0.60, 0.65, and 0.70) under the following conditions: MgO = 35%, GGBS = 45%, designed wet density = 700 kg/m 3 , and non-carbonated (0 day). SEM images indicate that all three groups exhibit a typical foamed structure dominated by nearly spherical pores. With increasing water-to-binder ratio, the pore walls tend to become thinner, and open pores and local pore coalescence become more evident. The histograms and fitted curves show that pore sizes in all groups are mainly concentrated in the range of 100–200 μm, with an approximately normal distribution, although the mean/median positions differ slightly among groups. The scatter plots and box plots further reveal that the w/b = 0.65 group has a more concentrated distribution with lower dispersion, indicating a relatively uniform pore structure. In contrast, the w/b = 0.60 and 0.70 groups show greater dispersion and a higher proportion of abnormally large pores. This suggests that an excessively low water-to-binder ratio may hinder bubble stability and uniform dispersion due to higher slurry viscosity, whereas an excessively high ratio tends to weaken the foam films and promote pore coalescence, leading to pore-structure coarsening. Differently designed wet densities Fig. 11 Pore size distribution of C-LFS at different water-to-binder ratios

Fig.  12  shows the pore size distribution characteristics and statistical results of C-LFS with differently designed wet densities (600, 700, and 800 kg/m 3 ) under the following conditions: MgO = 35%, GGBS = 45%, water-to-binder ratio = 0.65, and non-carbonated (0 day). SEM images show that all three groups display a nearly spherical foamed pore structure. As the wet density increases, the pore walls become thicker and more continuous, and the occurrence of open pores and pore coalescence is reduced. The histograms and fitted curves indicate that pore sizes in all groups remain mainly concentrated within 100–200 μm and follow an approximately normal distribution. The scatter plots and box plots further show that the 600 kg/m 3  group has greater dispersion and more abnormally large pores, reflecting the thinner pore walls and insufficient stability at low density, which makes bubble coalescence and defective pore formation more likely. In contrast, the 700–800 kg/m 3  groups exhibit a more concentrated pore-size distribution with fewer extreme values, indicating that increasing wet density can effectively improve pore-structure uniformity and pore-wall quality. Fig. 12 Pore size distribution of C-LFS at different wet densities

sections.heading: Hydration Productions
paragraphs: Using the representative mixture of 35% MgO and 45% GGBS (a water-to-binder ratio of 0.65 and a designed wet density of 700 kg/m 3 ), the phase assemblage of C-LFS and its evolution with carbonation age were analyzed by XRD and TG-DSC. As shown in Fig.  13 a and c, all samples exhibit a broad hump within 2θ = 20–40°, which is assigned to the amorphous gel framework dominated by C-(A)-S-H-type products. Distinct reflections at approximately 29.4° and 39.4°, together with weaker peaks near 43.1° and 47.5–48.5°, are attributed to calcite. Considering that the SP used in the present study is limestone-based, these calcite peaks in the 0-day specimen represent the baseline CaCO 3  contribution from SP and are further intensified after carbonation. In addition, reflections at about 18.6°, 38.0°, 50.8°, and 58.6° are assigned to brucite, indicating the hydration of MgO. Hydrated Mg carbonates potentially formed during carbonation, such as nesquehonite and hydromagnesite, are expected to generate weak or partially overlapping reflections around 13.6–15.2°, 21.2–23.1°, and 29.4–30.5°. However, in the present diffractograms these signals are not sufficiently resolved from the dominant calcite/brucite background for rigorous phase-by-phase quantification. Therefore, they are conservatively discussed here as Mg-carbonate-related products rather than as individually quantified crystalline phases (Jin et al.,  17 ; Zhang et al.,  39 ). Fig. 13 Carbonation-induced evolution of amorphous gel and carbonate products in C-LFS.  a  XRD patterns with single-Gaussian fitting of the amorphous hump over 20–40° after linear baseline subtraction,  b  TG-DSC curves,  c  normalized amorphous-hump quantification,  d  segmented TG mass loss in carbonate decomposition ranges

The corresponding TG-DSC curves further corroborate the above transformation (Fig.  13 b). The DSC heat-flow signal shown on the right-hand axis is presented in the original instrumental unit of mW/mg. In the low-temperature region (approximately 80–130 °C), the mass-loss mainly corresponds to evaporation of free water. The mass-loss and endothermic peak in the low-to-intermediate temperature range (approximately 120–250 °C) can be attributed to dehydration of gels and hydrated phases. A characteristic change associated with dehydroxylation of Mg(OH) 2  is observed in the range of approximately 380–460 °C. In addition, the mass-loss events in the ranges of approximately 450–600 °C and 700–850°C correspond to the decomposition of magnesium carbonates and CaCO 3 , but the mass-loss contribution in the 700–850 °C interval contains the baseline CaCO 3  contribution from SP; therefore, for the representative mix, only the incremental increase relative to the 0-day specimen was used to indicate additional CaCO 3  accumulation caused by carbonation. As the carbonation age increases, the mass-loss contribution within the carbonate decomposition ranges progressively increases, indicating that carbonation substantially enhances the carbonate content in the system. This enhancement is more clearly demonstrated by the segmented TG mass-loss analysis (Fig.  13 d). The mass-losses assigned to Mg-carbonate decomposition (450–600 °C) and CaCO 3  decomposition (700–850 °C) both increase with carbonation duration, confirming continuous accumulation of carbonate product. Notably, the simultaneous increase in carbonate-related mass loss and decrease in the amorphous hump metrics suggests that the microstructural evolution is not a simple pore-filling process, instead, it reflects a shift from a gel-dominated binding framework toward carbonate precipitation accompanied by gel destabilization. This provides a mechanistic basis for the observed trade-off between enhanced CO 2  mineralization and strength degradation under prolonged carbonation curing.

Fig.  14  shows clear microstructural differences in C-LFS at different carbonation ages. At 0-day carbonation, the matrix is mainly composed of flocculent gel, and abundant plate-like or layered crystals, identified as Mg-enriched hydration products [e.g., Mg(OH) 2 ], are observed on the pore-wall surfaces together with gel-like phases (C-(A)-S-H). The pore walls are relatively intact but remain rough. After 1 day of carbonation, fine particulate deposits and locally formed surface coverage layers appear on the gel and pore-wall surfaces, while the boundaries of the plate-like crystals become blurred. These features indicate the onset of carbonation reactions, during which Mg-carbonates (e.g., nesquehonite, hydromagnesite, and dypingite) and CaCO 3  nucleate and precipitate, producing an initial surface-covering effect. At 3-day carbonation, clustered particulate precipitates increase markedly and locally evolve into needle- and rod-like deposits, suggesting enhanced formation and aggregation of Ca- and Mg-carbonates (MgCO 3  and CaCO 3 ). Meanwhile, the pore-wall surface becomes more uneven and defective, implying progressive pore-wall destabilization and increased pore connectivity. At 5-day carbonation, carbonate-rich deposition layers become thicker and more continuous; however, open pores, pore coalescence and microcracks are more prominent, indicating that prolonged carbonation shifts the microstructural evolution from early-stage surface filling to pore-wall damage and cracking. Fig. 14 Carbonation-induced microstructural evolution and damage quantification of C-LFS (0, 1, 3, and 5 days),  a  microstructural constituents at 12,000 × magnification,  b  microcrack morphology at different carbonation ages at 250 × magnification,  c  pore-wall thickness,  d  crack length density

To further support the SEM observations, Fig.  14 b and c provides semi-quantitative metrics of microstructural damage. With increasing carbonation age, the pore-wall thickness exhibits a clear downward trend, while the crack length density increases continuously, confirming progressive thinning and cracking of the pore-wall framework. This quantitative evolution explains why carbonate precipitation does not translate into strength enhancement in highly porous foamed structures: although carbonates can locally deposit on surfaces, the load-bearing gel skeleton is gradually weakened and the thin pore walls become more susceptible to cracking and coalescence, ultimately facilitating macro-scale strength loss under prolonged carbonation curing.

These microstructural observations suggest that carbonation may induce pore-wall destabilization beyond surface precipitation. To interpret the strength loss under enhanced CO 2  uptake, the correlations between UCS and the evolution of pore structure and reaction products are discussed below.

sections.heading: Effect of Pore Structure on Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: Pore structure is an important characteristic because it affects porosity-dependent properties such as strength. To evaluate the influence of pore structure on UCS, the median values of D50 (median pore size), D90 (the size below which 90% of pores fall), and the roundness parameter R50 were used. Roundness is defined as the ratio of the minimum to the maximum diameter of an air void, and R50 represents the median roundness. Fig.  15  illustrates the effects of carbonation age and MgO content on the relationships between pore-structure parameters and UCS. As shown in Fig.  15 a, when carbonation duration increases from 0 to 5 days, the pore structure exhibits a trend of pore coarsening-roundness reduction, with D50 and D90 gradually increasing and R50 continuously decreasing. Meanwhile, UCS decreases from 1.132 to 0.722 MPa, showing consistent changes. Overall, D50 and D90 are negatively correlated with UCS because larger pores weaken the continuity of the load-bearing skeleton and intensify stress concentration. In contrast, R50 is positively correlated with UCS, as a lower roundness indicates more irregular pore shapes, which are more likely to form weak zones and promote earlier crack propagation. Fig.  15 b further shows differences among MgO contents. The 45% MgO group has larger D50 and D90 but smaller R50, corresponding to a lower UCS (0.893 MPa). This indicates that under high MgO conditions, the pore system more readily evolves toward a higher proportion of large pores and more irregular pore shapes. The resulting weak pore-wall regions and stronger stress concentration facilitate crack initiation and propagation, thereby accelerating macroscopic strength degradation. In general, although a high MgO content may enhance carbonation reactivity, its tendency to induce pore coarsening and pore-shape deterioration is more pronounced, ultimately undermining the integrity of the load-bearing skeleton. Fig. 15 Effects of carbonation age and MgO content on the relationships between pore-structure parameters and UCS:  a  Different carbonation ages,  b  different MgO contents

sections.heading: Influence of Microstructural Phase Evolution on Mechanical Performance
paragraphs: Fig.  16  shows the relationships between amorphous gel content, CaCO 3  content, and UCS. As the carbonation age increases, UCS continuously decreases, while the overall amorphous gel content also declines. This indicates that, during carbonation, the gel phases that dominate the load-bearing skeleton are progressively reduced or weakened, which is a direct cause of strength degradation. In contrast, the CaCO 3  content increases with carbonation, confirming that carbonation reactions proceed continuously. However, this increase does not result in strength improvement; instead, it coincides with the decline in UCS. This suggests that CaCO 3  formation mainly reflects the accumulation of reaction products and phase transformation, and it cannot effectively reconstruct a continuous gel network. Moreover, it may even offset the potential local pore-filling and densification effect by inducing gel decalcification, structural rearrangement, pore coarsening, or microcrack development. Fig. 16 Relationships between amorphous gel and CaCO 3  contents and UCS:  a  Amorphous gel content versus UCS,  b  CaCO 3  content versus UCS

sections.heading: Carbonation-Induced Strength-Loss Mechanism of C-LFS
paragraphs: Based on the macro-, meso-, and micro-scale results, carbonation curing does not improve the compressive strength of C-LFS at the same mix proportion and designed wet density; instead, the UCS decreases progressively with increasing carbonation age, although the measured values still satisfy the engineering requirements for subgrade embankment and subgrade-bed filling. This strength reduction becomes more pronounced under the combined condition of higher MgO dosage and longer carbonation duration. Integrating the macroscopic strength results with the mesostructural observations and microscopic characterization, it can be inferred that the dominant driving factor for the carbonation-induced strength loss is the chemical weakening of the gel-based load-bearing framework, whereas physical damage mainly acts as a coupled amplification pathway in the highly porous foamed architecture. Specifically, during carbonation, CO 2  continuously penetrates the pore network and dissolves into the pore solution, leading to the formation of carbonate species and a rapid decline in pore-solution alkalinity (Fig.  17 ). The reduced alkaline environment suppresses the sustained activation of GGBS and the late-stage hydration of MgO, thereby limiting the continued generation of strength-contributing gels. Meanwhile, carbonation also alters the chemical stability of the pre-existing gel framework, weakening its bonding and supporting functions within the pore-wall skeleton. As the chemically bonded framework progressively loses continuity and mechanical integrity, the thin-walled foamed structure becomes increasingly vulnerable to pore-wall thinning, crack propagation, pore coalescence, and brittle fracture, as evidenced by the mesoscopic pore deterioration and structural defects. Therefore, the macroscopic strength decline is not only primarily governed by physical pore damage alone but also essentially rooted in the chemically induced degradation of the gel-based load-bearing skeleton, with the intrinsic structural fragility of the foamed system further amplifying this weakening effect. Fig. 17 Evidence chain for carbonation-induced strength loss in C-LFS:  a  Isothermal calorimetry heat-flow curves,  b  cumulative heat release,  c  pH kinetics,  d  overlaid FTIR spectra

From an engineering perspective, the investigated C-LFS system is suitable for lightweight subgrade backfill within the wet-density range of 600–800 kg/m 3 . The 600 kg/m 3  level provides a stronger lightweight effect but is more vulnerable to carbonation-induced pore-wall deterioration, whereas the 700–800 kg/m 3  range offers better pore-wall integrity and strength retention and is therefore more favorable when mechanical reliability is prioritized. MgO acts as a key regulator of constructability and strength development: increasing MgO reduces flowability and shortens setting time, while the 28-day UCS exhibits a rise-then-fall trend, indicating an optimum dosage around 35% under the present mixture conditions. Carbonation curing markedly enhances CO 2  uptake and carbonate formation, but prolonged carbonation continuously reduces UCS; accordingly, carbonation should be applied in a controlled manner to balance carbon mineralization and mechanical performance rather than to maximize strength.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
paragraphs: Although the present study clarifies the trade-off between CO2 mineralization and strength loss in C-LFS, further work is still required before full engineering deployment. Future studies should optimize the curing boundaries, including pre-curing duration, CO 2  concentration, relative humidity, carbonation duration, and post-carbonation moist or sealed curing, so as to establish staged curing protocols that better balance carbon uptake and strength retention. In parallel, the binder chemistry should be refined by adjusting MgO reactivity and dosage, the GGBS and SP ratio, and possible auxiliary alkali- or Ca-bearing components, with the aim of maintaining a sufficiently alkaline environment while promoting a more stable gel-carbonate hybrid skeleton. In addition, long-term durability and field applicability should be verified through water-stability tests, immersion tests, wet-dry and freeze–thaw cycling, chemical attack resistance, volume stability evaluation, pilot-scale construction trials, and preliminary techno-economic assessment considering the regional cost and supply of MgO.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study develops a low-carbon lightweight foamed soil geomaterial for green geotechnical construction, using an all-solid-waste binder in which MgO, GGBS, and stone powder fully replace Portland cement. The material is designed for subgrade backfill improvement with wet densities of 600–800 kg/m 3 , enabling simultaneous solid-waste valorization and CO 2  mineralization potential. The main conclusions are as follows: C-LFS can be successfully prepared using a cement-free MgO-GGBS-SP binder system at target wet densities of 600–800 kg/m 3 , which constitutes a feasible engineering window for lightweight subgrade backfill. Within this range, the 700–800 kg/m 3  levels provide better pore-wall integrity and strength retention, whereas 600 kg/m 3  offers a stronger lightweight effect but is more sensitive to carbonation-induced deterioration. MgO is a key parameter governing both fresh-state behavior and strength development. Increasing MgO dosage decreases slurry flowability and markedly shortens the setting time. The 28-day UCS shows a rise-then-fall trend with MgO dosage and water-to-binder ratio, indicating the existence of an optimum parameter window. Under the present experimental conditions, the representative optimum combination is MgO = 35 wt.%, w/b = 0.65, and target wet density = 700 kg/m 3 , at which the 28-day UCS reaches 1.132 MPa. Carbonation curing significantly enhances CO 2  mineralization, with the CO 2  uptake reaching approximately 67.3 kg CO2/t after 5 days of carbonation. However, within the investigated carbonation range (15 days), no strength gain is obtained; instead, the 28-day UCS decreases continuously with increasing carbonation duration, and the reduction becomes more pronounced under the combined condition of high MgO dosage and prolonged carbonation. Even after 5 days of carbonation, the 28-d UCS remains at 0.752 MPa, which still satisfies the strength requirement for subgrade filling. The dominant mechanism behind the enhanced CO 2  uptake but reduced UCS is the carbonation-induced collapse of pore-solution alkalinity and the consequent weakening of the gel-based load-bearing skeleton. Suppressed sustained GGBS activation and late-stage MgO hydration, together with gel decalcification, pore-wall thinning, pore coarsening, and microcrack development, progressively destabilize the highly porous foamed structure. Therefore, carbonation should be regarded as a controlled mineralization strategy rather than a strength-enhancing curing route for this system. From an engineering perspective, MgO contents around 35 wt.% and wet densities of 700–800 kg/m 3  are recommended, while the combination of high MgO dosage and prolonged carbonation should be avoided when mechanical reliability is prioritized.
